title: Imputation-based Time-Series Anomaly Detection with Conditional Weight-Incremental Diffusion Models

problem.claim: Time-series anomaly detection models can become ineffective when anomalous points occur intensively in particular episodes.

gap.claim: Existing models are primarily trained on data dominated by normal points and do not adequately handle concentrated anomalies.

contributions.claim: DiffAD frames anomaly detection as a time-series imputation problem and uses a density-ratio strategy to flexibly select normal observations.
DiffAD introduces conditional weight-incremental diffusion for denoising-based imputation, preserving observed-value information and improving data generation quality.
DiffAD customizes a multi-scale state space model to capture long-term dependencies across episodes with different anomaly patterns.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly present DiffAD as a new approach for anomaly concentration scenarios.

author_reported_evidence.claim: On real-world datasets, the authors report that DiffAD performs better than state-of-the-art benchmarks.

narrative_sequence.summary: Normal-point-dominant training can fail when anomalies are concentrated in episodes.
DiffAD addresses the problem through a time-series imputation perspective and density-ratio-based selection of normal observations.
Conditional weight-incremental diffusion improves denoising-based imputation, while a multi-scale state space model captures long-term episode dependencies.
The authors report better performance than state-of-the-art benchmarks on real-world datasets.

source_observation.claim: Selecting normal observations with a density-ratio strategy is intended to adapt to different anomaly concentration scenarios.

interpretation.claim: When contamination patterns vary across episodes, adaptive observation selection may be more suitable than fixed partial- or complete-observation assumptions.

application.claim: Consider adaptive selection of presumed-normal observations when designing anomaly detection systems for data with uneven anomaly concentration.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish performance or applicability outside the reported settings.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the real-world datasets, evaluation metrics, or benchmark identities.
